detailedInstruction:
Welcome to C++ programming! C++ is a powerful, fast language used for games, systems, and more:

1. Open Visual Studio Code (VSCode)
2. Navigate to your workspace folder
3. Right-click in the file explorer
4. Select 'New File' from the context menu
5. Name the file 'hello.cpp' (note the .cpp extension)
6. Press Enter to create the file

Why .cpp extension: C++ files use .cpp (or .cc, .cxx). The 'pp' stands for 'plus plus'. C++ needs to be compiled before running, similar to Java but different from Python.
hint: Right-click in workspace, select 'New File', name it 'hello.cpp'
errorCorrection: Make sure the extension is .cpp, not .c or .txt

hint: Copy the code exactly - C++ is very picky about syntax
errorCorrection: Check for semicolons, correct spelling of 'iostream'

detailedInstruction:
C++ must be compiled before running. Let's compile it:

1. Save your hello.cpp file (Ctrl+S or Cmd+S)
2. Open terminal in VSCode (View → Terminal)
3. Compile with this command:
   g++ hello.cpp -o hello
   
   OR if g++ isn't installed:
   clang++ hello.cpp -o hello

What this does:
• 'g++' or 'clang++' - C++ compiler
• 'hello.cpp' - Your source file
• '-o hello' - Output executable named 'hello'

If successful, you'll see no errors and a new executable file will be created. If you see errors, read them carefully - they'll guide you to fix syntax issues.
errorCorrection: If g++ not found, try clang++ or install g++

detailedInstruction:
Now let's run your compiled C++ program:

1. In terminal, type:
   ./hello     (on Mac/Linux)
   OR
   hello.exe   (on Windows)

2. Press Enter

What happens:
• The executable file contains machine code
• Your operating system runs it directly
• Much faster than interpreted languages
• You should see 'Hello, World!' printed

Note the './' prefix on Mac/Linux - this tells the system to run the file in the current directory.
hint: Type './hello' on Mac/Linux or 'hello.exe' on Windows
errorCorrection: Make sure you compiled successfully first
